Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

vignette: Tien Nguyen was twenty-two when the jungle firestorm collapsed around his unit near the Ho Chi Minh trail. He remembered the sudden crack of incoming mortar, the way the earth buckled, and then the crushing weight of a fallen log and tangled barbed wire pinning his legs to the mud. Hands had grabbed his shoulders, fingers digging into his uniform as he struggled to breathe through the thick plume of burning rubber and wet soil that seeped into his nose. The shouting of nearby soldiers had felt like a physical wall, each harsh syllable vibrating against his ribs. In the years that followed, Tien had come to believe that the war had not truly ended; it had simply been waiting for the right moment to return. He started avoiding crowded loading docks and tight quarters, telling himself he was just preserving his peace, though he noticed how his shoulders remained permanently raised, how he scanned every doorway for shadows. By the time he took the warehouse floor job in his late forties, Tien had built a routine around quiet aisles and predictable shifts, but the environment itself became a quiet architect of his distress. On a humid Tuesday, the sudden hiss of a pallet jack's hydraulic release and the sharp tang of diesel exhaust cut through the air. Before he could step back, the olfactory cue unlocked a flood of detail-the same burning rubber, the same heavy mud, the same crushing weight across his chest-pulling the past directly into his present. He dropped his clipboard, breath catching as the memory returned. When the recollection fully surfaced, he felt so overwhelmed by the emotion that he had to stop moving, pressing his palms flat against a steel shelf to steady himself. Over the months that followed, this pattern hardened into habit. He began requesting the morning shift to avoid the midday forklift traffic, claiming it was for productivity, though he knew he was trying to outrun the very sensory cues that now fed the past into his present. The memory would surface without warning, a sudden and unfiltered recollection that left the details of that day stark and immediate. Because the memory returned so vividly, the ordinary warehouse environment instantly transformed into a threat landscape; what had been a simple aisle now felt like an enclosure, and the pressure of shrink wrap catching his wrist registered exactly as the restraint that had pinned him down. Tien had come to believe that if he stayed alert, he could keep the past at bay, but his hypervigilance only kept the loop spinning. His wife had left years earlier, citing his withdrawal, and now, working alone in the back corner of the distribution center, he found himself flinching whenever the warehouse doors groaned open. The consequences were concrete: he missed two safety audits, received a written warning, and stopped speaking to the shift manager who had asked him to attend a team briefing. The final straw arrived when a colleague's heavy hand landed on his shoulder during a routine handoff. The sudden physical restraint mirrored the weight of that day, and the memory flooded back with such clarity that he had to step out onto the hot asphalt just to catch his breath. What frightened him most was not the flashback itself, but the certainty that he was losing control of his own body in places where he used to feel capable. He had finally walked into the clinic because the warehouse had become a place of dread, and he could no longer ignore how the past was hijacking his present. He was hoping, more than anything, to find a way to untangle the threads that bound him, to sit through a shift without waiting for the ground to give way beneath him. He wanted to reclaim the quiet of his later years, but he was terrified that if he let his guard down, the war would step through the door again.
